title: Is the known exponent for distributed even-cycle detection optimal?
formal: For every fixed integer $k\ge3$, is $\widetilde\Omega(n^{1-1/k})$ a worst-case round lower bound for randomized detection of a simple cycle of length exactly 2k in the CONGEST model? The network is an arbitrary simple undirected n-vertex graph. Each vertex initially knows n, its distinct O(log n)-bit identifier, and its incident edges; each edge carries O(log n) bits per direction per synchronous round. If a cycle exists at least one vertex must output YES, and otherwise all must output NO. Require the joint answer to be correct with probability at least 2/3 on every input.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated lower bound for every fixed k at least three, or refute it for at least one fixed k. A randomized algorithm with a fixed improvement in the exponent for one such k would refute the conjecture. The k=2 case is already known and is not the open target.
context:
Cycle detection asks whether information about a bounded number of vertices can be assembled somewhere in the network. With unbounded messages, a constant-radius neighborhood suffices for a fixed cycle length. With limited messages, a vertex may learn that there are many short paths without having enough information to combine compatible paths into a cycle.

A simple six-cycle uses six distinct vertices. Walking across one edge and back three times is also a closed walk of length six, but is not a valid witness. Conversely, a graph containing a six-cycle may also contain triangles or four-cycles. Computing only the shortest cycle length would therefore not answer the exact-length existence question.

The algorithmic exponent changes with the fixed requested length. The conjecture predicts two-thirds for six-cycles, three-quarters for eight-cycles, and progressively larger exponents for longer fixed even cycles. Constants may depend on the length; the question is about how the communication cost grows with network size.

The best known upper bound already works deterministically even when each vertex must broadcast the same message to all its neighbors. The proposed lower bound concerns the stronger model allowing different messages to different neighbors. Establishing it would show that neither private randomness nor this extra communication flexibility improves the exponent.
why: I include this because it asks whether a simple pattern parameter determines a precise hierarchy of communication costs. The gap is not merely about derandomizing an algorithm: the upper bound is already deterministic, while the missing lower bound must exclude every randomized protocol in the stronger unicast model.
definitions: The cycle need not be induced: additional edges between its vertices are allowed. Local computation is unrestricted and random bits are private. Here $\widetilde\Omega(n^a)$ means a lower bound $\Omega(n^a/(\log n)^b)$ for some fixed b; constants may depend on k and the algorithm, but not n. A worst-case bound ranges over input graphs and identifier assignments. k is known to all vertices and is fixed before n grows.

progress.text: Censor-Hillel and coauthors give improved algorithms for small even cycles and show that, already for six-cycles, a lower bound $\Omega(n^{1/2+\alpha})$ for fixed positive alpha would imply major circuit lower bounds.
Fraigniaud, Luce, Magniez, and Todinca obtain randomized $O(n^{1-1/k})$-round detection for every fixed k.
The same authors obtain deterministic $O(n^{1-1/k})$ rounds in Broadcast CONGEST. Their conclusion explicitly leaves optimality open for every k>2.
